exercise_group.instruction: In Exercises 1 and 2, let $$A = P D P^{- 1}$$ and compute $$A^{4}$$ .
In Exercises 3 and 4, use the factorization $$A = P D P^{- 1}$$ to compute $$A^{k}$$ , where $$k$$ represents an arbitrary positive integer.

problem.paragraph: $$\begin{bmatrix} a & 0 \\ 3 \left(\right. a - b \left.\right) & b \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 3 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} a & 0 \\ 0 & b \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ - 3 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$$

exercise_group.instruction: In Exercises 5 and 6, the matrix $$A$$ is factored in the form $$P D P^{- 1}$$ . Use the Diagonalization Theorem to find the eigenvalues of $$A$$ and a basis for each eigenspace.

Diagonalize the matrices in Exercises 7–20, if possible. The eigenvalues for Exercises 11–16 are as follows: (11) $$\text{λ} = 1,2,3$$ ; (12) $$\text{λ} = 1,4$$ ; (13) $$\text{λ} = 5,1$$ ; (14) $$\text{λ} = 3,4$$ ; (15) $$\text{λ} = 3,1$$ ; (16) $$\text{λ} = 2,1$$ . For Exercise 18, one eigenvalue is $$\text{λ} = 5$$ and one eigenvector is $$( - 2,1,2)$$ .

In Exercises 21–28, $$A,P$$ , and $$D$$ are $$n \times n$$ matrices. Mark each statement True or False (T/F). Justify each answer. (Study Theorems 5 and 6 and the examples in this section carefully before you try these exercises.)

problem.paragraph: (T/F) $$A$$ is diagonalizable if $$A = PDP^{- 1}$$ for some matrix $$D$$ and some invertible matrix $$P$$ .
(T/F) If $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ has a basis of eigenvectors of $$A$$ , then $$A$$ is diagonalizable.
(T/F) $$A$$ is diagonalizable if and only if $$A$$ has $$n$$ eigenvalues, counting multiplicities.
(T/F) If $$A$$ is diagonalizable, then $$A$$ is invertible.
(T/F) If $$A$$ is diagonalizable, then $$A$$ has $$n$$ distinct eigenvalues.
(T/F) If $$AP = PD$$ , with $$D$$ diagonal, then the nonzero columns of $$P$$ must be eigenvectors of $$A$$ .
(T/F) If $$A$$ is invertible, then $$A$$ is diagonalizable.
$$A$$ is a $$5 \times 5$$ matrix with two eigenvalues. One eigenspace is three-dimensional, and the other eigenspace is two-dimensional. Is $$A$$ diagonalizable? Why?
$$A$$ is a $$3 \times 3$$ matrix with two eigenvalues. Each eigenspace is one-dimensional. Is $$A$$ diagonalizable? Why?

$$A$$ is a $$4 \times 4$$ matrix with three eigenvalues. One eigenspace is one-dimensional, and one of the other eigenspaces is two-dimensional. Is it possible that $$A$$ is not diagonalizable? Justify your answer.

$$A$$ is a $$7 \times 7$$ matrix with three eigenvalues. One eigenspace is two-dimensional, and one of the other eigenspaces is three-dimensional. Is it possible that $$A$$ is not diagonalizable? Justify your answer.
Show that if $$A$$ is both diagonalizable and invertible, then so is $$A^{- 1}$$ .
Show that if $$A$$ has $$n$$ linearly independent eigenvectors, then so does $$A^{T}$$ . [Hint: Use the Diagonalization Theorem.]

$$A$$ factorization $$A = P D P^{- 1}$$ is not unique. Demonstrate this for the matrix $$A$$ in Example 2. With $$D_{1} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{rr} 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 5 \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ , use the information in Example 2 to find a matrix $$P_{1}$$ such that $$A = P_{1}D_{1}P_{1}^{- 1}$$ .
With $$A$$ and $$D$$ as in Example 2, find an invertible $$P_{2}$$ unequal to the $$P$$ in Example 2, such that $$A = P_{2}D P_{2}^{- 1}$$ .
Construct a nonzero $$2 \times 2$$ matrix that is invertible but not diagonalizable.
Construct a nondiagonal $$2 \times 2$$ matrix that is diagonalizable but not invertible.

exercise_group.instruction: Diagonalize the matrices in Exercises 39–42. Use your matrix program’s eigenvalue command to find the eigenvalues, and then compute bases for the eigenspaces as in Section 5.1.

problem.paragraph: $$\det (A - \text{λ} I) = \text{λ} ^{2} - 3 \text{λ} + 2 = ( \text{λ} - 2)( \text{λ} - 1)$$ . The eigenvalues are $$2$$ and $$1$$ , and the corresponding eigenvectors are $$\textbf{v}_{1} = \begin{bmatrix} 3 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix}$$ and $$\textbf{v}_{2} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}$$ . Next, form $$P = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 1 \\ 2 & 1 \end{bmatrix} , D = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} , \text{and} P^{- 1} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & - 1 \\ - 2 & 3 \end{bmatrix}$$

So, $$\textbf{v}_{1}$$ and $$\textbf{v}_{2}$$ are eigenvectors for the eigenvalues 1 and 3, respectively. Thus $$A = P D P^{- 1} , where P = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 2 \\ 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix} and D = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 \end{bmatrix}$$

Yes, $$A$$ is diagonalizable. There is a basis $$\{\textbf{v}_{1},\textbf{v}_{2}\}$$ for the eigenspace corresponding to $$\text{λ} = 3$$ . In addition, there will be at least one eigenvector for $$\text{λ} = 5$$ and one for $$\text{λ} = - 2$$ . Call them $$\textbf{v}_{3}$$ and $$\textbf{v}_{4}$$ . Then $$\{\textbf{v}_{1},\textbf{v}_{2},\textbf{v}_{3},\textbf{v}_{4}\}$$ is linearly independent by Theorem 2 and Practice Problem 3 in Section 5.1. There can be no additional eigenvectors that are linearly independent from $$\textbf{v}_{1}$$ , $$\textbf{v}_{2}$$ , $$\textbf{v}_{3}$$ , $$\textbf{v}_{4}$$ , because the vectors are all in $$\mathbb{R}^{4}$$ . Hence the eigenspaces for $$\text{λ} = 5$$ and $$\text{λ} = - 2$$ are both one-dimensional. It follows that $$A$$ is diagonalizable by Theorem 7(b).
